Statement 1: Definition of Newton's Law of Cooling — Statement
Statement 2: Theorem related to Newton's Law of Cooling — Statement

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ Newton's law says temperature is proportional to time. ✅ It says the RATE of temperature change is proportional to the temperature difference: $\frac{d\theta}{dt} \propto (\theta - \theta_0)$. The solution is exponential, not linear.  ·  ❌ Newton's law applies to all temperature differences. ✅ It is only accurate when $\theta - \theta_0 < 30°\text{C}$ approximately. For large differences, use Stefan-Boltzmann: rate $\propto \theta^4 - \theta_0^4$.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Application of Newton's Law of Cooling — Statement

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ The constant $k$ is the same for all bodies. ✅ $k$ depends on the body's surface area, texture, and the surrounding medium. Two identical bodies in different environments have different $k$ values.  ·  ❌ A black body cools slower than a shiny body. ✅ A black/dull body has HIGHER emissivity and cools FASTER. This is why radiators are painted black and survival blankets are shiny (to retain heat).

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: **Statement:** The rate of loss of heat of a body is directly proportional to the difference between the body's temperature ($\theta$) and the surrounding temperature ($\theta_0$), provided the temperature difference is small (typically $< 30°\text{C}$).  ·  **Mathematical form:** $\frac{dH}{dt} = -k(\theta - \theta_0)$, where $k > 0$ is a constant depending on the body's properties and surface area. The negative sign indicates heat is LOST (temperature decreasing).

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Connection of Newton's Law of Cooling — Statement to other topics

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Newton actually stated his law of cooling in 1701, based on experiments with thermometers cooling in air. It is one of the earliest examples of a differential equation in physics.  ·  The exponential decay form of Newton's law of cooling is mathematically identical to many other natural processes: radioactive decay, RC circuit discharge, population decay, and drug elimination from the bloodstream.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **In terms of temperature rate:** Since $dH = mc\,d\theta$, we get $\frac{d\theta}{dt} = -\frac{k}{mc}(\theta - \theta_0) = -K'(\theta - \theta_0)$, where $K' = \frac{k}{mc}$ is the cooling constant.  ·  **The constant $k$:** $k$ depends on (i) the nature of the body - material, surface texture, emissivity; (ii) the surface area exposed to surroundings; (iii) the nature of the surrounding medium (air, water). A blackened surface cools faster than a polished one.  ·  **Applicability condition:** Newton's law is an APPROXIMATION valid only when $(\theta - \theta_0)$ is small. For large temperature differences, Stefan-Boltzmann radiation law ($\frac{dH}{dt} \propto \theta^4 - \theta_0^4$) must be used.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Newton's law and Stefan-Boltzmann law give the same result always. ✅ They agree when $(\theta - \theta_0)$ is small. For large differences, Stefan-Boltzmann gives a much faster cooling rate (proportional to $T^4$).  ·  ❌ The surrounding temperature must be zero for Newton's law. ✅ $\theta_0$ is the temperature of the surroundings (e.g., room temperature ≈ 25°C). The law uses the DIFFERENCE $(\theta - \theta_0)$, not absolute temperature.  ·  ❌ Newton's law applies to heating as well as cooling. ✅ Yes! If $\theta < \theta_0$, the body GAINS heat and the rate is positive: $\frac{d\theta}{dt} = +K'(\theta_0 - \theta)$. The same law describes both heating and cooling.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ The body reaches room temperature in finite time. ✅ The exponential function $e^{-K't}$ approaches zero asymptotically but never reaches zero. The body gets arbitrarily close to $\theta_0$ but never exactly reaches it.  ·  ❌ The cooling curve is a straight line. ✅ The cooling curve $\theta(t)$ is an exponential decay, not a straight line. The slope $d\theta/dt$ decreases with time. Only the plot of $\ln(\theta - \theta_0)$ vs. $t$ is a straight line.  ·  ❌ The half-life depends on the initial temperature. ✅ The half-life $t_{1/2} = \ln 2/K'$ depends ONLY on the cooling constant, not on $\theta_i$. Each half-life reduces the excess by half, regardless of the starting excess.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ A larger $K'$ means slower cooling. ✅ A larger $K'$ means FASTER cooling. $K' = k/(mc)$ — larger $k$ (better heat transfer) or smaller $mc$ (less thermal inertia) gives faster cooling.  ·  ❌ The exponential solution only works for cooling, not heating. ✅ The same equation $\theta(t) - \theta_0 = (\theta_i - \theta_0)e^{-K't}$ works for both. For heating, $(\theta_i - \theta_0)$ is negative, so $\theta(t)$ increases toward $\theta_0$.  ·  ❌ After one time constant, the body has cooled halfway. ✅ After one time constant $\tau$, the excess is $1/e \approx 36.8\%$ of its initial value, not 50%. The half-life is $t_{1/2} = \tau \ln 2 \approx 0.693\tau$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ You can use the approximate method (average rate) for large temperature differences. ✅ The approximate method $\frac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t} = K'(\theta_{avg} - \theta_0)$ is only accurate for small temperature intervals. For large intervals, use the exact exponential formula.  ·  ❌ Identical cooling conditions mean the bodies cool at the same rate of temperature fall. ✅ Identical conditions mean equal heat-loss constant $k$. The temperature fall rates can differ if the heat capacities ($mc$) differ.  ·  ❌ If two bodies cool at the same temperature rate, they must be the same material. ✅ They must have the same heat capacity ($mc$), but different combinations are possible: a small mass of high-$c$ material can equal a large mass of low-$c$ material.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ The calorimeter's heat capacity can be ignored in the method of cooling. ✅ The calorimeter absorbs/releases the same heat as the liquid. For accurate results, include $W$ (water equivalent) in the equation.  ·  ❌ Two bodies with the same mass always cool at the same rate under identical conditions. ✅ Same mass is not enough — they must also have the same specific heat (same $mc$). Different materials with the same mass cool at different rates.  ·  ❌ The method of cooling requires equal masses of the two liquids. ✅ It requires equal volumes in identical calorimeters. The masses should be measured and used in the calculation. Equal volumes don't guarantee equal masses if densities differ.
